Abstract
Diabetes is a widespread chronic metabolic disorder that affects a substantial portion of the global population and 
requires diligent management and continuous medical supervision. Traditional glucose monitoring methods often 
involve invasive procedures that cause discomfort and increase the risk of infection. With the rapid advancements of 
the Internet of Things (IoT) and cloud computing, healthcare is evolving for early disease detection and personalized 
treatment solutions. The aim of this research is to develop a system based on the Internet of Things (IoT) for non-invasive 
diabetes detection using Photoplethysmography (PPG) signals. Our system leverages machine learning models, such as 
XGBoost, Random Forest, Logistic Regression, and SVM, to accurately classify diabetic patients using statistical features 
collected from PPG signals and metadata. To ensure model robustness, we employed a fivefold cross-validation approach. 
The hardware technology includes a portable, cost-effective system with a simple NIR sensor and a high-performing 
ESP32 module that minimizes user discomfort and ensures easy integration. Deployed on the Amazon Web Services 
(AWS) cloud platform, our system enables real-time data collection and analysis, providing users with a convenient web 
application for monitoring their diabetic status. The performance of the developed system has been tested with two 
different datasets: the PPG-BP dataset and the Mazandaran dataset, achieving 87.88% and 90% accuracy, respectively. 
The results demonstrate the potential of the designed system to revolutionize diabetes management by providing a 
non-invasive, accessible, and accurate solution for early-stage detection.
Article Highlights
•	 A non-invasive Internet of Things-based system using Photoplethysmography signals for early diabetes detection.
•	 Integration with cloud technology ensures real-time monitoring and user convenience.
•	 Achieves up to 90% accuracy with cost-effective hardware and advanced machine learning algorithms.

1  Introduction
Diabetes has emerged as a leading cause of death. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), approximately 
422 million people globally currently live with diabetes, with a disproportionate burden impacting lower and middle-
income countries [1]. It causes the death of nearly 1.5 million people each year. Both the number of cases and the 
prevalence of diabetes have been steadily increasing over the past few decades.
This chronic condition manifests as persistently elevated blood glucose concentrations, stemming from pancreatic 
dysfunction in insulin secretion or cellular insensitivity to insulin action [2]. This metabolic imbalance can have severe 
consequences, potentially leading to damage to vital organs and increasing the risk of serious complications such 
as heart attacks, kidney failure, and cerebrovascular events.
Type 1 diabetes (T1D) and type 2 diabetes (T2D) represent the two most prevalent classifications. T1D, an 
autoimmune condition, results from the permanent destruction of insulin-producing cells in the pancreas. 
Consequently, individuals with T1D require lifelong insulin therapy for survival. In contrast, T2D is characterized by 
either insufficient insulin production or impaired insulin action by target tissues. T2D can be prevented or controlled 
through lifestyle modifications and medical interventions [3]. Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is a separate form 
affecting women during pregnancy [4].
Early detection and management of diabetes are essential to prevent complications and improve patient well-
being [5]. While current methods like finger pricking and continuous glucose monitors (CGMs) provide valuable data, 
they are invasive and inconvenient for frequent monitoring. Traditional blood glucose meters (BGMs) require finger 
pricking, a process that can be both uncomfortable and irritating for patients who need frequent monitoring [6]. 
CGMs provide a more continuous solution but still necessitate finger pricks for calibration and are often expensive 
and bulky. Consequently, the financial burden, discomfort, and potential risks associated with CGMs have limited 
their widespread implementation for frequent blood glucose monitoring.
The limitations of existing methods underscore the importance of developing reliable, non-invasive solutions. 
Non-invasive diabetic detection technologies hold immense potential to revolutionize diabetes care by offering a 
more comfortable and convenient approach [7]. These technologies aim to eliminate the need for invasive procedures, 
such as finger pricking, while maintaining precision, reliability, and minimizing side effects [8].
Photoplethysmography (PPG), a non-invasive optical method, quantifies variations in blood volume in the 
microvascular bed of tissues [9]. This signal analysis can provide vital physiological information, such as heart rate, 
oxygen saturation, and blood pressure. Beyond these applications, PPG has emerged as a promising tool for assessing 
cardiovascular health and detecting early signs of diabetes [10]. Studies have demonstrated that PPG signals can 
indicate arterial stiffness through pulse wave velocity (PWV) measurements, which show how flexible arterial walls 
are [11]. Since people with diabetes have higher stiffness levels, PPG is useful in early stage diabetes detection.
In addition, the study suggests that automated diagnostic systems can help address the shortage of medical 
expertise in developing countries [12].
The convergence of the Internet of Things (IoT) and cloud computing within the healthcare domain has the 
potential to significantly improve efficiency, serviceability, and flexibility among medical devices [13]. This integration 
facilitates real-time data acquisition, analysis, and the generation of personalized recommendations for diabetes 
management, enabling earlier detection and improved patient outcomes [14].Data security and privacy are crucial in 
IoT-based health monitoring. Secure data transmission requires strong encryption, authentication mechanisms, and 
compliance with healthcare regulations [15]. Energy efficiency is a critical factor in IoT-based healthcare systems [16].
This study aims to develop a comprehensive, real-time, and user-friendly IoT-based system for the detection of 
diabetes. By integrating a cost-effective and portable hardware system equipped with a simple NIR sensor and a 
high-performance ESP32 module, we aim to create an accessible tool for individuals to effectively monitor their 
diabetic status. Our approach integrates statistical features extracted from PPG signals with demographic information, 
offering a perspective on the prediction of diabetes. Using advanced machine learning algorithms, including XGBoost, 
Random Forest, Logistic Regression, and SVM, we strive for high accuracy and reliability in our predictions. The 
system facilitates seamless data collection, processing, and analysis through an end-to-end framework, ensuring a 
user-friendly experience. In addition, cloud technology is used to improve scalability, accessibility, and integration 
with existing hardware components.
The rest of the paper is organized as follows: Sect. 2 presents the literature, and the detailed proposed methodology 
is presented in Sect. 3. Section 4 demonstrates the results, including performance evaluation of four ML algorithms

2  Literature review
Several studies have explored the application of machine learning algorithms to non-invasively collected 
photoplethysmography data, utilizing IoT-enabled technology to identify individuals with diabetes [17].
The intelligent glucose measuring device (iGLU) improves blood glucose prediction accuracy by using NIR spectroscopy 
and intelligent algorithms. Auto-Regressive Moving Average (ARMA) models have been applied to extract glucose-related 
features from PPG signals of diabetic and non-diabetic participants [18].
The study [19] utilized XGBoost and logistic regression (LR) models to analyze morphological characteristics extracted 
from single PPG beats, achieving an accuracy of 70% in diabetes classification. In [20], the authors achieved an average 
accuracy of 84.62% in diabetes detection by applying 1D Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to analyze features 
extracted from short-time segments of PPG signals. The article [21] predicted the risk of developing type 1 diabetes with 
a dataset comprising 306 individuals by using various machine learning models, including Decision Trees, Deep Neural 
Networks, and XGBoost. This study also emphasized the importance of Explainable AI techniques, such as LIME, for 
enhancing the interpretability of predictions, a crucial factor for clinical decision-making in diabetes management [22]. 
However, due to the limited sample size, the generalizability of these findings to broader populations may be limited. 
Yilmaz et al. [23] applied five machine learning algorithms, including KNN, logistic regression, decision trees, SVM, and 
random forest, for classifying two types of diabetes using Python. Among these, the Random Forest algorithm achieved 
the highest performance, with a 96% accuracy rate and 94% precision and sensitivity in diagnosing early-stage diabetes.
In [24], the application of machine learning algorithms also demonstrated to predict diabetes using the Pima Indian 
dataset from the UCI repository, which includes data from 768 patients with attributes such as glucose levels and BMI. 
Since this study used only demographic data, their predictive result may have been limited due to the exclusion of 
valuable information that could be derived from PPG signals. Furthermore, the study [25] was limited by its exclusion of 
PPG signals from their analysis, despite utilizing various machine learning algorithms, including Adaboost, AutoML, and 
Random Forest, to classify diabetes status based on physiological data collected through sensors.
An non-invasive rehabilitation platform proposed to enable physical therapy exercises outside healthcare centers. 
It integrates a modified fuzzy PID control scheme and multiple sensors for adaptive, stable rehabilitation, along with 
torque, positioning. The system demonstrates the potential of wearable IoT technologies with embedded sensors to 
facilitate continuous health monitoring outside clinical environments [26].
An IoT-based smart clothing system designed for continuous monitoring of health parameters, such as heart rate, body 
temperature, walking steps, and motion by integrating sensors like AD8232 (ECG), MPU6050 (motion), and MAX30205 
(temperature). A dual mode power management system with sleep mode for energy efficiency and wake-up mode for 
continuous data transmission is used. The system includes a web-based platform that enables remote access to health 
data. The limitations of the system include the absence of predictive machine learning models, limited battery life, lack

The DiaFog system is a portable platform that combines deep learning, fog computing, and cloud services to enable 
remote diabetes diagnosis. Despite its advantages in speed and energy efficiency, its diagnostic accuracy across diverse 
populations remains a concern. Another solution is a urine-based IoT system designed for home-based monitoring, using 
wireless transmission and AI to identify diabetes markers. However, its accuracy is influenced by hydration levels and 
requires frequent calibration. Fog-assisted healthcare systems utilize wearable sensors and fog computing to efficiently 
process diabetes data and transmit securely cloud messages [7].
A fog-assisted IoT system for continuous health monitoring in diabetic patients with cardiovascular disease integrates 
sensors to measure blood glucose, ECG, body temperature, humidity, and air quality. The system processes data at the 
edge of the network using fog computing and reduces latency. The wearable sensor nodes are capable of operating for 
up to 141 h on a 1000 mAh battery. Data security is strengthened through lightweight cryptographic algorithms, ensuring 
secure transmission between sensors and fog nodes. The limitations of the system include battery life constraints, 
usability challenges for elderly users, limited integration of contextual and physiological data, and reliance on stable 
internet connectivity [28].
The authors of [4] developed an IoT-based diabetic prediction system that incorporates KNN as a machine learning 
model to classify diabetic severity using photoplethysmography (PPG) features. The research [29] proposed a patient 
health monitoring system using IoT and Machine Learning for early detection of diabetes. The system employs various 
wearable sensors to collect real-time patient data, including temperature, pulse rate, and blood pressure. This study 
focuses only on pregnant women and does not utilize PPG signals, which limits its generalizability.
Similarly, the study [30] presented a diabetic patient monitoring system using an IoT framework based on NodeMcu. 
The system utilizes a glucose sensor to collect blood glucose data and transmit them to the cloud for storage and analysis. 
Other physiological measures of the subjects were not incorporated into the system.
So, future research could explore integrating additional sensors and investigate the reliability of the IoT framework 
in real-world settings.
Conclusively, in [31], an IoT-based system proposed for diabetes prediction using gait analysis. Their system embedded 
accelerometers and gyroscopes in smart shoes to collect gait data, including acceleration and angular velocity, during 
walking. This data was then classified as normal or abnormal gait patterns using a Linear Regression model, achieving an 
accuracy of 83% in differentiating between diabetic and non-diabetic gaits. While promising for non-invasive diabetes 
risk assessment, the study acknowledged limitations such as data collection restricted to indoor environments.
However, our study addresses two key limitations, as illustrated in Table 2, identified in the existing literature. Despite 
the promising results of machine learning-based approaches for diabetic detection using PPG signals, many existing 
studies lack real-time monitoring capabilities due to the absence of an IoT infrastructure [19–32]. Additionally, some 
existing IoT-based systems for diabetic detection, while utilizing machine learning models, lacked reliability, especially 
when cloud integration was required. These systems often relied solely on demographic information, neglecting the 
valuable insights that could be gained from PPG signal [25–31].
The proposed method offers several key advantages over previous work. Firstly, it leverages the valuable insights from 
PPG signals, a crucial aspect often overlooked in previous studies that primarily relied on demographic data. Secondly, the 
integration of IoT infrastructure enables real-time data collection and transmission, facilitating continuous monitoring and 
early intervention [33]. Furthermore, the utilization of cloud computing ensures seamless data management, scalability, and 
easy integration with existing healthcare systems [34]. Finally, the evaluation of our system on two distinct datasets (PPG-BP

3  Methodology
Figure 1 illustrates the overall methodology for classifying non-diabetic and diabetic groups. To accurately classify non-
diabetic and diabetic patients, we selected two comprehensive datasets containing PPG signals and metadata information 
about the participants.
After preprocessing the signals to remove noise, we extracted key features and developed a robust classifier model using 
a combination of four machine learning algorithms. The final machine learning models were deployed, integrating IoT and 
cloud technology to provide predictions to users through a combined hardware and software system. The Machine learning 
system development process is depicted in Fig. 2.
3.1  Dataset selection and description
PPG-BP dataset We utilized a publicly accessible dataset from a study conducted at Guilin People’s Hospital in China, which 
included physiological information and PPG data from 219 patients [35].
PPG signals were acquired from the fingertips of resting patients using an infrared transmission method with a 905 nm 
light source and a 1 kHz sampling rate. Three 2.1-s segments, each containing 2100 samples, were recorded from each 
patient. The dataset included metadata such as age, weight, height, body mass index (BMI), arterial blood pressure (ABP), 
and a unique patient identifier.
For this study, we classified the subjects into two groups: non-diabetes and diabetes. The non-diabetic group consisted of 
40 healthy subjects, excluding all patients with any stage of hypertension or cerebrovascular disease. In contrast, the diabetic 
group included all 39 patients diagnosed with diabetes. Post-data collection, the signal quality index (SQI) was calculated to 
assess the quality of PPG signals using the following equation:

Mazandaran dataset We employed another publicly accessible dataset provided by the research team at 
the University of Science and Technology in Mazandaran, Behshahr, Iran [38]. The dataset consists of 67 raw PPG 
signals collected from 23 individuals, which is effective for our research as it allowed us to explore patterns in PPG 
signals associated with blood glucose levels. PPG signals were captured from the index finger’s first band using a 
pulse sensor with a 550-nm green-colored optical transmitter at 2175 Hz sampling rate. Data was obtained under 
controlled conditions to ensure signal integrity. Each signal sample was captured with a duration of 674.621 s. The 
dataset provides comprehensive demographic details, including age, gender, height, weight, and invasive blood 
glucose levels measured using the Accu-CheckTM self-monitoring device.
Similar to the first dataset, we classified patients into non-diabetic and diabetic categories. A glucose level of 
126 mg/dL or greater indicates type-2 diabetes [39]. We obtained 17 PPG signals from 12 diabetic patients based 
on this glucose leveland 40 PPG signals from 11 healthy subjects in the non-diabetic group.

3.2  Preprocessing
During data acquisition, PPG signals are often contaminated by various types of noise, including motion artifacts, 
muscle noise, and baseline wander. These contaminants can distort the PPG signal, leading to inaccuracies in 
subsequent analyses and interpretations.
To ensure the signal’s amplitude consistency, the PPG signal is typically normalized by adjusting its amplitude to a 
standard scale before filtering. An FIR band pass filter with a passband of 0.5 to 15 Hz and an order of 81 is designed 
to suppress noise and extract relevant physiological information. A balance between sharp transition and noise 
reduction was achieved by carefully selecting filter coefficients using the window method. Raw and filtered PPG 
signals are shown in Fig. 5.
In this analysis, FIR filters are preferred over IIR filters due to their inherent stability, phase linearity (preserving the 
shape of the waveform), and reduced sensitivity to coefficient quantization errors [40].
To ensure the suppression of unwanted noise components, spectral analysis of the processed signal was performed 
using the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), as shown in Fig. 6.

The prediction of diabetes is based on the information derived from the features. Essentially, this technique enhances 
the ability to detect diabetes accurately and efficiently, showcasing the potential of merging a features-oriented 
approach with a simple machine-learning technique for improved diagnostics.

3.4  Machine learning algorithms
Model selection To classify subjects by diabetic severity, we selected four supervised machine learning algorithms: 
Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Random Forest (RF), Logistic Regression (LR), and Support Vector Machine 
(SVM). They were chosen for their ability to handle statistical features, robustness, and suitability for hardware 
implementation. These algorithms were then implemented and evaluated using the scikit-learn Python library.

Data preparation We employed stratified fivefold cross-validation to prevent bias and ensure balanced class 
distribution. This approach divided the dataset into five equal subsets and iteratively trained and tested the model on 
different subsets.
Hyperparameter tuning To optimize model performance, we conducted hyperparameter tuning using random 
search and stratified fivefold cross-validation. This process helped identify the optimal hyperparameters for each model, 
minimizing the risk of overfitting [41].
Model evaluation The final models were evaluated using a comprehensive set of performance metrics: accuracy, 
sensitivity, specificity, F1-score, positive predictive value, and area under the ROC curve. We assessed the overall 
performance of each classifier by averaging the performance metrics across all cross-validation iterations.
3.5  IoT and cloud integration
In this study, we develop and deploy an IoT-based, real-time, and robust diabetic detection system, integrating a 
machine learning (ML) model with hardware. We selected Amazon Web Services (AWS) as the cloud platform due to its 
exceptional infrastructure, ease of use, high performance, open accessibility, and seamless integration with hardware. 
Leveraging cutting-edge technology and AWS’s cloud infrastructure, the system operates efficiently with minimal setup 
and maintenance, making it accessible to many users.
The system has two core components: hardware and software. By using NIR sensors, the wearable hardware system 
can be attached to the subject’s finger for comfortable capturing of PPG signals. The software component integrates a 
web application and backend server for real-time monitoring. The IoT and cloud integration process is depicted in Fig. 10.
ML deployment To make a system that detects if a subject is a diabetic patient or not, two phases are required. At first, 
we developed a robust machine learning model (as discussed above) by using the Python framework. This model was 
then implemented on an AWS EC2 instance using a Flask API, enabling real-time classification and immediate feedback 
to the web application.
Hardware system/ESP32 For building the whole prediction system, the ESP32 microcontroller, a cost-effective and 
versatile device, collects PPG signals from the user’s fingertip. This enables real-time, non-invasive monitoring and precise 
assessment of diabetic severity, facilitating timely interventions and improved healthcare discussions between doctors 
and patients.

User interface The web application acts as a communication bridge between the device and the remote server. PPG 
signal data is transmitted from the hardware to the application via Wi-Fi. The user interface includes multiple fields for 
entering demographic information. Upon receiving PPG signals and demographic data from the user, the web application 
displays real-time prediction results, as illustrated in Fig. 11.
Backend server and processing The remote server, visualized within the “Cloud" block in Fig. 1, is responsible for 
data preprocessing and classification. It filters PPG signals to remove noise and extracts the most relevant features. 
These features are then fed into the best-performing machine learning model for classification. The server saves the 
classification results and transmits them back to the web application.
Network communication The application handles communication between the backend server and the user interface. 
PPG data and demographic information were transmitted to the server in JSON format via HTTP POST requests. The server 
processes the data, classifies diabetic severity, and returns the results as a JSON object. The web application displays 
the results to the user. The server raises an error to the user if any issues, such as network errors or invalid data, occur 
during the process. The application’s primary objective was to provide users with an intuitive interface for leveraging 
the proposed classification algorithm.

The above system is designed following a complete four-layered IoT architecture [42] as shown in Fig. 12. The 
functions of each layer as depicted in Fig. 12 are described below:
1. Perception layer: This layer consists of the ESP32 micro-controller connected with a near-infrared (NIR) PPG 
sensor. So, this layer helps to capture physiological signals from the user’s fingertip.
2. Network layer: The ESP32 transmits the acquired PPG signals wirelessly to the AWS IoT Core via a secure Wi-Fi 
connection. This layer ensures reliable communication between edge devices and cloud services.
3. Edge and Cloud Layers layer: The AWS IoT Core serves as an edge computing gateway, forwarding incoming PPG 
data to an AWS Lambda function for preliminary pre-processing and feature extraction. The preprocessed features 
are transmitted to an AWS EC2 instance, where the machine learning model is deployed via a Flask API. This layer 
handles intensive computations, AI-driven classification, and secure data storage [42].
4. Application layer: This layer provides the interface between the users and backend system, allowing users to 
enter demographic details, visualize results, and receive automated notifications by email. Different types of attacks 
and their corresponding solutions for each IoT layer are shown in Table 3.

4  Performance analysis
This section presents a comprehensive analysis of the experimental findings obtained by applying various machine 
learning models to two datasets for the classification of diabetic severity. The results are analyzed in terms of 
classification performance, Receiver-Operating Characteristic (ROC)–Area Under the Curve (AUC) curve, confusion 
matrix, and feature importance.
4.1  Analysis of Guilin dataset
Performance metrics, including accuracy, F1-Score, precision, recall, ROC-AUC, and specificity, are summarized in 
Table 4. XGBoost achieved the highest F1 score (88. 235%) and AUC (96. 3235%), followed by Random Forest (F1 score: 
85. 7145%, AUC: 87.6838%), Logistic regression (F1 score: 83.975%, AUC: 90.7243%) and SVM (F1 score: 83.333%, 
AUC: 81.9853%).
Figure 13 depicts the ROC curves for four models shows in this study. The XGBoost model exhibited the highest 
AUC value, indicating superior discriminative performance, as validated through fivefold cross-validation.
The confusion matrices, depicted in Fig. 14, further highlight the strong performance of XGBoost and Random Forest, 
with a high number of correct predictions and a low number of incorrect predictions. The confusion matrices visually 
represent the models’ classification accuracy, enabling a detailed analysis of true and false positives and negatives. So, 
this analysis is crucial for identifying areas where the model excels and where improvements could be made.
Feature importance analysis was conducted to identify the most influential predictors of diabetes. Figure 15 shows 
the top eight features for XGBoost and Random Forest classifiers. The results indicate that statistical features related 
to signal morphology, such as kurtosis, skewness, and Mean absolute deviation, as well as patient metadata like age, 
BMI, and weight, significantly contributed to model performance. These findings suggest that these features are 
crucial in differentiating between diabetic and non-diabetic individuals.

4.4  Comparative study
Table 6 presents a comparative analysis of our research with existing studies on diabetic detection using PPG signals 
and demographic information. Previous studies primarily focused on either machine learning-based approaches 
using PPG signals or IoT-based systems relying solely on demographic information.
Studies by [19, 20], analyzing the application of machine learning to PPG signals for diabetic detection, did not 
incorporate IoT-based systems for real-time monitoring. Moreover, they used waveform or signal features, while our 
approach employed statistical features, resulting in enhanced performance with a reduced number of input variables.
IoT-based systems developed by the previous studies [25, 29], while enabling continuous monitoring, overlooked 
the significance of PPG signals, relying solely on demographic data.
Our system surpasses previous studies in several key areas by combining PPG signals, demographic information, 
IoT technology, and advanced machine learning algorithms. Our approach offers a comprehensive, real-time, and 
user-friendly solution for diabetes detection, achieving a remarkable 90.00% prediction accuracy.
5  Discussion
This study presents a non-invasive IoT-based system for diabetes detection, addressing the growing demand for 
accessible diagnostic solutions. By integrating IoT technology with machine learning algorithms, the system offers 
a cost-effective method for monitoring diabetic status using PPG signals. The hardware design prioritizes ease of 
use to minimize patient discomfort during signal acquisition, while the software ensures seamless operation with 
minimal setup requirements.
Performance evaluation demonstrated promising results, achieving 87.88% and 90.00% accuracy in two datasets.

capabilities. However, several challenges need further attention to ensure broader applicability and improved 
reliability. Signal interference caused by motion artifacts and environmental noise remains a concern, as variations 
in physiological conditions can impact the accuracy of the classification model.
Although our system handles security, scalability, connectivity, and real-time processing, the challenges related to 
interoperability between different IoT devices and cloud platforms require further optimization. In addition, regulatory 
compliance with healthcare standards, such as HIPAA and GDPR, remains crucial for safe deployment [15]. Moreover, 
cloud-based processing introduces latency concerns that could affect real-time decision making. These limitations 
highlight the need for further advances to refine the system.
6  Conclusions
This research introduces an IoT-based non-invasive system for early diabetes detection using PPG signals and machine 
learning. The proposed system demonstrates high accuracy that makes it a viable solution for real-world healthcare 
applications. By combining statistical feature extraction with machine learning-based classification, the system effectively 
identifies diabetic conditions, offering a promising alternative to traditional diagnostic methods.
Despite its good performance, certain challenges must be addressed. To enhance system performance, future 
research will focus on expanding the size of the dataset by incorporating a more diverse population and additional 
physiological parameters. Furthermore, advanced signal processing techniques such as adaptive filtering and noise 
reduction algorithms will be implemented to minimize motion artifacts and environmental noise. In addition, deep 
learning techniques will be investigated to optimize classification performance in larger datasets.
To overcome the challenges of IoT-cloud integration, research will focus on optimizing data processing and 
transmission strategies. Implementing edge computing solutions will help reduce latency by shifting some computational 
tasks to local devices. Incorporating multilayer authentication mechanisms will enhance data security. In addition, the 
development of standardized interoperability frameworks will facilitate seamless communication between IoT devices, 
cloud platforms, and healthcare systems. To improve accessibility in resource-limited environments, offline data storage 
using Bluetooth-based solutions and LCD integration will be explored to ensure that the system functions even with 
limited internet connectivity.
By bridging the gap between technology and healthcare, this system has the potential to improve diabetes 
management through early detection and proactive intervention. With continued advancements in security, scalability, 
and accessibility, the system can be further optimized for both clinical and personal health monitoring applications.

Abstract: Diabetes is a widespread chronic metabolic disorder that affects a substantial portion of the global population and requires diligent management and continuous medical supervision. Traditional glucose monitoring methods often involve invasive procedures that cause discomfort and increase the risk of infection. With the rapid advancements of the Internet of Things (IoT) and cloud computing, healthcare is evolving for early disease detection and personalized treatment solutions. The aim of this research is to develop a system based on the Internet of Things (IoT) for non-invasive diabetes detection using Photoplethysmography (PPG) signals. Our system leverages machine learning models, such as XGBoost, Random Forest, Logistic Regression, and SVM, to accurately classify diabetic patients using statistical features collected from PPG signals and metadata. To ensure model robustness, we employed a fivefold cross-validation approach. The hardware technology includes a portable, cost-effective system with a simple NIR sensor and a high-performing ESP32 module that minimizes user discomfort and ensures easy integration. Deployed on the Amazon Web Services (AWS) cloud platform, our system enables real-time data collection and analysis, providing users with a convenient web application for monitoring their diabetic status. The performance of the developed system has been tested with two different datasets: the PPG-BP dataset and the Mazandaran dataset, achieving 87.88% and 90% accuracy, respectively. The results demonstrate the potential of the designed system to revolutionize diabetes management by providing a non-invasive, accessible, and accurate solution for early-stage detection. Article Highlights • A non-invasive Internet of Things-based system using Photoplethysmography signals for early diabetes detection. • Integration with cloud technology ensures real-time monitoring and user convenience. • Achieves up to 90% accuracy with cost-effective hardware and advanced machine learning algorithms.
